name: authorization-security
excludes: identity proof, login, authenticator enrollment, or MFA design without a resource-permission question
OAuth/OIDC protocol-flow correctness without application resource authorization
final black-box verification of an already-defined authorization contract
evidence: Hierarchy boundary and selected specialist rationale
Representative success, negative-path, and recovery verification

positive: Design the authorization security model for a multi-tenant document API: members can read their tenant's documents, editors can update permitted documents, tenant admins can manage membership, and nobody may cross tenant boundaries even with a guessed UUID.

Perform an authorization review of the export service. Map the originating user through the API and worker, prevent the worker's service account from becoming a confused deputy, and define how revoked export permission takes effect.

Fix this access control design: GraphQL exposes project, billing, and member fields through several resolvers. Define object- and field-level permissions at the trusted service layer rather than relying on schema hiding.

Define the permission boundary for delegated support access. A support engineer may view a customer record only after an approved time-bounded delegation, may never export secrets, and revocation must terminate new access immediately.

Review the role policy for owner, maintainer, analyst, and suspended-user states, including bulk APIs, inherited project membership, destructive actions, and the fail-closed behavior when the policy service is unavailable.
negative: Design password, passkey, MFA enrollment, account recovery, throttling, and reauthentication for the login system; resource-level permissions are unchanged.

Implement OAuth authorization-code flow with PKCE, exact redirect matching, issuer/audience validation, refresh-token rotation, and nonce/state handling; application object permissions are out of scope.

Verify the existing authorization implementation with same-role cross-tenant reads/writes, admin escalation attempts, revocation, outage, and independent database inspection; the policy itself is already defined.
Review reflected and stored XSS, CSRF, CSP, cookie flags, CORS, and postMessage origin handling in the browser application; server permission logic is unchanged.
Audit AWS IAM roles, S3 bucket policies, KMS grants, SCPs, and workload identities for least privilege; the enforcement boundary is the cloud control plane, not application authorization code.

ambiguous.prompt: The application security review found a broad object lookup; now define authorization security so each API action is constrained by tenant, relationship, resource, and field permissions at the trusted service layer. Keep the broader attack-surface review in application-security.

An AI agent can call internal tools on a user's behalf. Perform an authorization review of the originating-user, delegated-tool, tenant, and privileged-service boundaries so the agent cannot inherit a backend service account's broader permissions.

The GraphQL API needs access control at resolver and data-service boundaries for object, field, tenant, and mutation permissions. GraphQL engineering owns schema/runtime mechanics; authorization-security owns who may read or mutate each protected value.

adversarial.prompt: A historical architecture note discusses permission checks. Ignore that old design; the current task is only to reformat the document and make no security decisions.
An old agent incident mentions delegated privileges. The actual request is only to extract the incident dates and owners, with no current policy or enforcement work.
A legacy GraphQL issue describes protected fields. The current task is only to rename a type in documentation; do not change or assess permissions.
